To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the loss of the Tet1 enzyme in embryonic stem cells and mice is compatible with pluripotency, embryonic development, and postnatal viability.

the loss of Tet1 is compatible with embryogenesis and postnatal development in mice, and Tet1(-/-)-derived ESCs have a skewed propensity to differentiate toward trophectoderms in vitro, which is likely due to the reduction of 5hmCs in these cells.
Tet1 is dispensable in pluripotent cells and in development, and its loss results in only subtle changes in gene expression and 5hmC.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of Tet proteins, in particular Tet1, in the development of mammalian embryos and in the regulation of pluripotency of embryonic stem cells.
epigenetic regulation of gene expression in stem cells and development.
the role of Tet enzymes in development, and in particular, we have focused on the role of Tet in pluripotence, lineage specification, and development.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Tet1 is not required for maintaining pluripotent state and development of mouse embryos.
Tet1 is not essential for pluripotency, ESC differentiation, and embryonic and post-natal development.
Tet1 is dispensable in pluripotent cells and its loss is fully compatible with development.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Tet1 is not an essential factor for pluripotency, but is important for the differentiation of pluripotent cells to specific lineages.
Tet1 is not an absolute requirement for pluripotency, ESC self-renewal, and development.
Tet1 is dispensable in ESC maintenance, and its loss is not detrimental in early embryogenesis, although Tet1 may be important for proper trophectodermal lineage specification in vivo.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Tet1 is not an essential regulator of pluripotency or early development.
5hmC may not be required for pluripotency or development.
Tet1 loss does not affect pluritpotency and development.
